paras: The shooting of Sol Russell took place on a Saturday in August 1895 in Brick Store district near Covington, Georgia, when Frank Patrick wounded Russell, a Black man, while Patrick and several other men were trying to arrest him. Russell was hit in the face and eyes with bird shot and was jailed in Covington, where doctors thought he might lose an eye.

According to the Covington Star, Patrick and several other men surrounded the house where Russell was staying "for the purpose of arresting him." The Star said Russell ran out with a Winchester rifle and, seeing Patrick first, "deliberately" fired at him. Before Russell could fire again, Patrick returned fire and struck him in the face and eyes with bird shot; Patrick is not reported to have been hit. The report does not say what Russell was to be arrested for, nor whether Patrick held any office.

Russell was held in the Covington jail and treated there by Drs. J. A. Wright and W. D. Travis, who thought he would probably lose one eye. No report of a charge, hearing or trial for either man appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from a single paragraph credited to the Covington Star and reprinted on Aug. 21, 1895, in the "Georgia and Florida" column of the Savannah Morning News, among items on crops, lightning strikes and local businesses. The paragraph gave only the arresting party's version, called Russell "a desperate negro," and ended by describing him as "a bad negro" who had "not been out of the 'gang' but a short while." No account from Russell's side and no coverage in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Shooting of Sol Russell
bases: A group led by Frank Patrick surrounded a house to arrest Sol Russell and Patrick shot and wounded him in an exchange of fire; the report gives no official standing for the group and describes no attempt to kill him outside the arrest (A1).

Russell was wounded, not killed, and was taken to jail in Covington; the several men who surrounded the house acted 'for the purpose of arresting him', and whether they had lawful authority is not stated (A1).
The only report is one paragraph in the Savannah Morning News credited to the Covington Star (A1); no other white or Black paper was found.
